answer_text:
Let

\[
I=\int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-(\ln x)^2/2}\,dx.
\]

Use the substitution

\[
t=\ln x,\qquad x=e^t,\qquad dx=e^t\,dt.
\]

As \(x\) goes from \(0\) to \(\infty\), \(t\) goes from \(-\infty\) to \(\infty\). Thus

\[
I=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-t^2/2}e^t\,dt
=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{t-t^2/2}\,dt.
\]

Complete the square:

\[
t-\frac{t^2}{2}
=-\frac12(t^2-2t)
=-\frac12\bigl((t-1)^2-1\bigr)
=\frac12-\frac{(t-1)^2}{2}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
I=e^{1/2}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-(t-1)^2/2}\,dt.
\]

Let \(u=t-1\). Then \(du=dt\), and the limits remain \(-\infty\) to \(\infty\):

\[
I=e^{1/2}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-u^2/2}\,du.
\]

Using the standard Gaussian integral

\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-u^2/2}\,du=\sqrt{2\pi},
\]

we get

\[
I=e^{1/2}\sqrt{2\pi}=\sqrt{2\pi e}.
\]

As for the Gamma function, this is fundamentally a Gaussian integral, not a Gamma-type integral of the form \(\int_0^\infty t^{a-1}e^{-t}\,dt\). However, since

\[
\Gamma\left(\frac12\right)=\sqrt{\pi},
\]

one can trivially rewrite the result as

\[
I=\sqrt{2e}\,\Gamma\left(\frac12\right).
\]

So the value is elementary, and any Gamma-function representation is only a trivial use of \(\Gamma(1/2)\).

\[
\boxed{\int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-(\ln x)^2/2}\,dx=\sqrt{2\pi e}=\sqrt{2e}\,\Gamma\left(\frac12\right)}
\]
